en: From the edge of Keng-Dyngsha,
From the face of Keng-Norko,
From the plain of snowy Ala-Too,
From the banks of Karkyra,
From the plain of Ükürchü,
From the fork of Üch-Kapkak,
From beneath Aygyr-Zhal,
Where he pastured at Chok-Tabylgy
And tethered his great black horse,
The infidel son of Kalday,
The youngest of sixty nobles,
That infidel son of Kalday,
The warrior Khan Kongurbay—
Spurring on Telküröng,
I reached the Manchu khan;
Ezkara, khan of the Manchus,
And Kongurbay, khan of the shaven-headed,
I buried them and rode on.
I cut off his head
And laid it before the foolish hero
As an offering.
I raised a mighty commotion.
Zhamgyrchy’s Akbala,
With dimpled mouth and camel-calf eyes,
With rounded hips and broad hair ornaments,
With her stately, flashing eyes,
Was the finest of women.
She was Khan Zhamgyrchy’s daughter;
If she wished, she was as sacred as the Night of Destiny.
For the warrior who had served,
Your sister-in-law was the maid destined for me.
Because I had avenged our father,
Because I had struck down Kongurbay
And laid him flat upon his back,
Zhamgyrchy’s Shayymbet
Clothed the lovely Akbala, my beloved,
In patterned gray silk,
And mounted her on a smooth-gaited pacer,
Making the hem of that silk robe
So wide that it swept the ground.
She had grown graceful as a doe,
Her hair coiling around her head;
She had matured like a young deer,
Her hair winding about her feet.
Her dowry was complete and displayed,
And she stretched proudly like a white doe,
Too reserved even to speak.
Without holding counsel
About that unfortunate beauty,
Kanchoro did not give her to me.
When God struck the bloodthirsty man,
He stirred the nation and gathered the people,
Then decreed that the son of Almambet
Should take that lovely Akbala.
When he decided it so,
He exalted Külchoro as a lion
And burned me, leaving me diminished;
Thus he began my grief.
Of that radiant beauty,
The companion I thought was mine—
Listen, my friend Kyyaz—
Thus he left me bereft.
Unable to equal Akbala,
Unable to shatter the world and prove myself no lesser,
Rather than remain without a wife,
Rather than become one with the black earth,
I raged and rushed away,
Offended by this deed
Of Manas’s foolish son.
I meant to slay men and scatter the people,
And depart;
Hearing that Kyyaz of Zheti-Özön
Was a true hero, I meant
To come away to you.
I meant to reach
The very root of that bloodthirsty man.
I have many things to tell;
Not once, but a thousand times,
That ill-starred butcher,
That deceiver who ruined the people,
Has stripped me of honor.
When we campaigned against China,
When we seized and slaughtered
The finest armor-clad Chinese,
When we drove forth and killed
The strongest Chinese in their jackets,
Zhamgyrchy’s daughter Akbala
Was brought by Shayymbet, and we took her.
We hoped to gather khojas and mullahs,
And have them wed her to me;
While I cherished that hope,
That arrogant deceiver
Refused to heed our words,
Refused to give Akbala to me,
And gave her to Külchoro.
My heart burned and turned to embers.
Unable to become a mighty champion who breaks armies,
Unable to prove Akbala’s equal,
I blazed and burned with anguish;
That was when my heart first turned against him.
Gather as spoil the noble bride, fair Saykal,
And bring her here;
And as for the other widowed bride,
Give Akbala to me.
That proud woman
I shall make my junior wife.
If she will not give me her heart,
If she will not obey my word,
I shall dress her in coarse felt,
Make her know a low slave’s lot,
And send her behind the sheep;
I shall make her fetch wood and water,
Heap misery upon her and torment her,
And demand her years while she still lives.
If the shrew gives me her heart,
I shall erase all her sorrow
And give that radiant unfortunate
A name honored above all.
I shall make her shine like the rising moon
And captivate every watching heart.
That proud woman,
That surpassingly beautiful infidel,
Shall wear rows of yellow keys,
Keys fashioned wholly of gold,
Fastened to her sash.
I shall have her tended in the shade,
Rally the nation and gather the people,
And make her my cherished wife.
I shall stir and gather the people
And make the dark-eyed woman my wife.
If that woman gives me her heart,
I shall have ninety beasts slaughtered for her feast
And name her Ayym.
I shall have a separate palace built for her,
And have emeralds and rubies cut
For the crown-ring of every palace,
And set into its roof-ring;
This is what I shall do for the bride.
But if that woman disobeys,
I shall have the herdsmen beat her
And the shepherds abuse her;
I shall not let her wear rawhide shoes,
Nor let her hem touch the ground;
I shall make her drive camels in the rain
Until her eyes blaze with torment.
If I do not make her the slave of slaves,
If I do not torture the life from her,
May I die no longer Kanchoro,
May I sink as though never born!
As for this warrior Semetey,
I shall torment and round up his people,
Torment his mother and destroy her;
If I do not slaughter their leaders
And extinguish them like a fire,
When I rear up in wrath,
Will not black stone crumble to flour,
Unable to withstand my fury?
When they provoke
The rage of mighty Kanchoro,
Will not the whole world be shattered?
When he rises in fury,
Will he not suck the age dry as a strand of hair?
Is this not what happens when he grows wrathful?
When angered, if I raise my battle cry,
Can the whole world endure it?”
So spoke Kanchoro.
The finest among those in ample robes,
The foremost among those in ample robes,
Your heroic, fierce mother
Stood before Khan Kanchoro,
Along with all the wrestlers who served him.
All were armed with daggers,
Their arms were fearsomely strong;
All were eminent champions.
If even one champion broke loose,
No man could escape his reach.
If you ask of former days,
They were Semetey’s champions;
If you ask of the present,
They were Khan Kanchoro’s champions.
They numbered forty-one.
Whoever became khan,
It was the custom of those ill-fated champions
To go over to him.
They made Kanchoro khan,
And forty champions remained with him;
Like wolves, those forty champions
Tore apart whomever he named.
Those forty champions humbled
Anyone who met their gaze.
At their khan’s command, those forty champions
Unleashed tumult.
Like eagles, those forty champions
Seized whomever he ordered them to seize.
Those forty champions stirred the nation,
Slaughtered the people, and remained.
When he pointed out a victim, those forty champions
Brought him down like a boar.
Striking terror into every spirit,
With every oath they swore,
Those forty champions remained.
Khan Kanchoro’s fame
Spread throughout the Kyrgyz people;
The menace of the forty champions
Spread throughout the world.
At the word “Speak!” the forty champions
Stood ready to pounce;
At the cry “Strike!” the forty champions
Charged with a roar.
Those forty champions stood
At Khan Kanchoro’s side.
Damn those forty champions!
They caused many a mighty outrage.
Ah, Kanykey in her old age,
The blessed, fierce-hearted woman,
The dark beauty,
The noblest of women,
The graceful one with long hair,
The finest of all womankind—
They heaped humiliation upon your lord
And inflicted unbearable suffering
Upon your unfortunate mother Kanykey.
Not merely his mother, but his sanctuary,
She had nursed the renowned, bloodthirsty prince
Until the Five Argali constellation had set,
Giving him the breast five times along the road.
She had a young mare slaughtered,
Made him bite off
The mare’s honeyed fat with his teeth
And suck it with his tongue,
Nurturing his little life into strength,
Restoring his frail soul,
Giving him drops when he was fading,
Reviving him when he was dying,
Raising him in her arms until he grew strong.
Eighty-year-old Kanykey,
As though she were Kanchoro’s own mother,
Had tended him in this way—
Semetey, her gray-maned prince.
Now that Kanykey had grown old,
They subjected the old woman of the palace
To monstrous humiliation.
The forty champions brought her before the khan:
“Here is the slave who shall serve you,” they said,
And delivered her to him.
Bridling with fury,
When he saw Kanykey,
His eyes flared like fire;
His bloodlust seized him,
His front teeth were as broad as a gate,
Teeth unlike those of ordinary men;
He ground them separately.
From Kanchoro’s mouth
A blue flame billowed.
Bereft of her young camel,
The aged woman Kanykey
